questions.problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations in two variables, represented by the matrix equation $Ax=0$ in the usual way. Given that the system has a unique zero solution, which of the following statements are true?

- $det(A)\ne 0$
- $A$ is not invertible
- The system $Ax=b$ has no solution for some $2\times 1$ column vectors $b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

Also, we are told that the third part of the invertible matrix theorem is true. So, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement I is true by the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false by the second part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement I is true.

questions.problem:
Let 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 
Which of the following statements are true?

- $det(A)=0$
- $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b$
- ${A}^{-1}$ does **not** exist
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is true by the second part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false. According to the first part of the invertible matrix theorem, the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ must exist.

Finally, only statement II is true.

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}6x+2y=1 \\ -3x+ky=-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is a constant. Complete the following statement so that it is true: 

If the system's coefficient matrix is invertible then $\text{__________}\,.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements. 

According to the invertible matrix theorem, if

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}]
$$

is invertible then $det(A)\ne 0.$    

Additionally, the unique solution to $Ax=0$ is $⟨0,0⟩$ and 

$$
[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

has exactly one solution, which is the intersection point of the two lines $6x+2y=1$ and $-3x+ky=-2.$ 

Finally, notice that if $k=-1$ then 

$$
det[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}]=det[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]=6\cdot (-1)-2(-3)=0.
$$

So, if $A$ is invertible,  then $k\ne -1.$

Therefore, the true statement is as follows:

*If the system's coefficient matrix is invertible, then the lines $6x+2y=1$ and $-3x+ky=-2$,  intersect at exactly one point.*

- The lines $a_{11}x+a_{12}y=b_1$ and $a_{21}x+a_{22}y=b_2$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $\det(A) \neq 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot k-(-2)\cdot (-2) \\  & =k-4,\end{aligned}
$$

where $k - 4 \neq 0$ if $k \neq 4.$ 

So, since the fifth part in the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the second part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be exactly one solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$

- Statement III is true by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement III is true.
